title: Shallow copy
body:
Copying the outer container and **not** the things inside it. The copy is a new object whose
properties point at exactly the same objects the original's did.

This is the answer to the question at the bottom of [[Array Functions]]:

```js
const found = drivers.filter(d => d.id < 5);
found[0].name = "ready";
alert(drivers[0].name);          // "ready"
```

`filter` built a genuinely new [[Array]]. But the elements in it are the same three objects
that are in `drivers`, so writing through one name is visible through the other. `map`,
`slice`, `concat`, `Object.assign`, and the spread `{...obj}` / `[...arr]` are all shallow in
exactly this way.

| Operation | Copies | Shares |
|---|---|---|
| `arr.slice()`, `[...arr]` | the array | every element object |
| `{...obj}`, `Object.assign({}, obj)` | the top level | every nested object |
| `arr.map(d => ({...d}))` | array and one level of element | anything nested inside an element |
| `structuredClone(obj)` | everything | nothing |

A **deep** copy duplicates the whole graph. `structuredClone` is the built-in way;
`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` is the old trick and silently destroys functions, `undefined`
values, and dates, because [[JSON]] holds none of those.

The reason this matters at all is that in JavaScript objects are held by reference and
primitives by value, so `=` copies a reference for the first and a value for the second. That
is the same distinction [[Copying]] draws in C++, where the fix is a copy constructor rather
than `structuredClone`, and the same one behind `Node* next` versus `Node next` in
[[Pointer]]. See [[Objects]].
